objects: large noisy matrix; sparse signal; classical SVD
assumptions: Significant structure occupies a small subset of a large noisy matrix.
conclusion: Classical subspace iteration accumulates variance and computational cost from structureless cells, motivating sparse SVD.
scope: High-dimensional noisy matrices with concentrated signal.
span: The problems our approach addresses are the following: For large noisy matrices in which the significant structure is concentrated in a small subset of the matrix X XX, the classical algorithm outlined above produces estimates with large variance due to the accumulation of noise from the majority of structureless cells (Shabalin and Nobel, 2010). In addition to the detriment for statistical estimation, involving large numbers of structureless cells in the calculations adds unnecessary computational cost to the algorithm.

assumptions: Observed noisy data matrix; target rank and threshold procedure supplied.
conclusion: FIT-SSVD fits the sparse low-rank approximation through thresholded subspace iterations that estimate singular vectors simultaneously.
scope: Main fitting procedure; stopping is based on successive subspace projections, not an asserted global optimum.
span: We present a new computational approach to approximating a large, noisy data table by a low-rank matrix with sparse singular vectors. The approximation is obtained from thresholded subspace iterations that produce the singular vectors simultaneously, rather than successively as in competing proposals.

assumptions: Sparse signal; two-way data matrix; robustness to non-Gaussian tails sought.
conclusion: FIT-SSVD initialization adapts Johnstone and Lu dimensionality reduction to the two-way case while weakening reliance on normal noise.
scope: Sparse initialization, not equivalence of the complete methods.
span: The algorithm is motivated by Johnstone and Lu (2009) who obtained a consistent estimate for principal components under a sparsity assumption by initially reducing the dimensionality. We adapt their scheme to the two-way case, and we weaken its reliance on the assumption of normal noise which in real data would result in too great a sensitivity to even slightly heavier tails than normal.

assumptions: Gaussian noise in model (1); appropriately chosen parameters; specific parameter space of the cited companion theory.
conclusion: The authors report that their algorithm attains the asymptotic minimax lower-bound rate under Gaussian noise and appropriately chosen parameters.
scope: Companion-paper result summarized here; the parameter space and full theorem conditions are not supplied in this statement.
span: For Gaussian noise in the model (1), we (Yang et al., 2011) showed that our algorithm with appropriately chosen parameters achieves the rate of the minimax lower bound. In other words, in a specific parameter space, our algorithm is asymptotically optimal in terms of minimizing the maximum possible risk over the whole parameter space.

objects: strict rank r; trailing small singular values
assumptions: Theory assumes an exactly rank-r signal.
conclusion: The authors identify a disconnect between strict-rank theory and empirical use with additional small singular values.
scope: No guarantee for trailing-rank signals is supplied.
span: Further, there exists still a partial disconnect between asymptotic theory and practical methodology: The theory requires a strict rank r rr model, whereas by all empirical evidence the algorithm works well in a “trailing rank” situation where real but small singular values exist.

objects: heavy-tailed noise; isolated outlying cells; robustification
conclusion: Heavy-tailed noise can generate random factors from single outliers, and the authors provide no theoretical framework justifying their robust modifications.
scope: Empirical robustness choices remain theoretically unvalidated in this paper.
span: Finally, there is a robustness aspect that is specific to sparse SVD approaches: heavier than normal tails in the noise distribution generate “random factors” caused by single outlying cells. While we think we have made reasonable and empirically successful choices in drawing from the toolkit of robustness, we have not provided a theoretical framework to justify them.

objects: orthogonal sparse singular vectors; simultaneous singular subspaces
assumptions: FIT-SSVD estimates leading left and right subspaces simultaneously.
conclusion: FIT-SSVD yields orthogonal sparse singular vectors, unlike the Witten et al. sparse SVD proposal.
scope: Structural comparison; no equivalence of objectives is claimed.
span: Our approach is to estimate the subspaces spanned by the leading singular vectors simultaneously. As a result, our method yields sparse singular vectors that are orthogonal, unlike the proposals by Witten et al. (2009) and Lee et al. (2010a).
